# Did a Bad Ballot Cost Bill Nelson the 2018 Senate Race?
# DUE MONDAY, NOVEMBER 2 AT NOON

In 2018, Republican Rick Scott defeated Democrat Bill Nelson for the U.S. Senate in Florida by only 10,033 votes, the closest Senate election in the history of the state. Afterward there were reports that a badly designed ballot in Broward County, the second-largest county in the state and one of its most Democratic, led some voters to skip the Senate race entirely. See, for example, the _New York Times_ article [here](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/09/upshot/florida-senate-race-broward-undercount.html) or the _Washington Post_ article [here](https://www.washingtonpost.com/outlook/2018/11/12/how-badly-designed-ballot-might-have-swayed-election-florida/).

A copy of the actual ballot is available [here](https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_official_sample_ballots,_2018). The Senate race was printed in the lower-left corner under a long block of instructions, and it seems plausible that voters missed it. When voters vote in some races on a ballot but not others we call that an **undervote**.

Suppose NBC hires you as a data consultant to determine whether there is evidence consistent with the claim that voters in Broward County missed the Senate race, and whether there were enough of them to have changed the outcome. This is an observational question: nobody randomly assigned ballots to counties. So we will use the three comparisons from Session 15 and then the correlation and regression tools from Session 16.

Recall that problem sets are graded by completion. I want you to try to figure things out on your own, with friends, or with help from me or Alex. The point is to understand what the code is doing and what the results mean.

HINT: Nothing here is intentionally tricky. 

You can also use AI to help you. But use it to help, don't outsource your thinking and agency to a machine. If you want to be capable you need to be able to work _with_ AI.

Fill in the answers in the spots below. Test things out using `Run Current Chunk` and then, when everything works, `Knit` from above - `Knit to PDF` is best. Make sure you save the name of this file to contain your VUNET ID!

NOTE: if it is not compiling for you send the document to AI and ask it to help you debug it! Figure out what went wrong and then go ahead.

The questions are in *italics*. Put your written answers after each question and your code in the answer chunk. When I ask what you observe, tell me what the number means!

## The data

Keep this Rmd and `florida_georgia.csv` in the same folder.

Each row is a county in Florida or Georgia. The variables record the votes for the Democratic and Republican candidates in the 2016 presidential and Senate races and the 2018 Senate and governor races. Georgia had no Senate race in 2018, so those columns are `NA` for Georgia.

| Variable | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `state` | `"FL"` or `"GA"`. |
| `county` | County name. |
| `fips` | The county's five-digit Census code. Broward County is `"12011"`. |
| `PresDemVote2016`, `PresRepVote2016` | Votes for Clinton and Trump in November 2016. |
| `SenDemVote2016`, `SenRepVote2016` | Votes for the Democratic and Republican Senate candidates in 2016. |
| `SenDemVote2018`, `SenRepVote2018` | Votes for Nelson (D) and Scott (R) for Senate in 2018. |
| `GovDemVote2018`, `GovRepVote2018` | Votes for Gillum (D) and DeSantis (R) for governor in 2018. |
| `PresDemPct2016` | Clinton's share of the two-party presidential vote in 2016 (votes for Clinton divided by votes for Clinton or Trump). |
| `SenDemPct2018` | Nelson's share of the two-party Senate vote in 2018 (votes for Nelson divided by votes for Nelson or Scott). |

NOTE: All counts are votes for the two major-party candidates only. Minor-party and write-in votes are not included.

## Where the data came from

County election returns compiled for this course. Presidential returns are from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab, *County Presidential Election Returns 2000-2020*, Harvard Dataverse, <https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/VOQCHQ>. Senate and governor returns are from official state results as compiled in the course's county election file. `florida_georgia.csv` keeps the Florida and Georgia counties and the 2016 and 2018 races used here.
